items.title: Base Models Can Detect Hidden Intentions that Prompted Classifiers Miss
items.content:
TL;DR

The Persona Selection Model (PSM) posits that post-training selects a persona the model learned during pre-training. Subliminal Learning (Cloud et al.) showed that models can impart covert signals (like "love of owls") into semantically unrelated outputs (like strings of numbers), and that students training on these outputs inherit those traits.

By using base pre-trained models with an appropriate header, a method I call persona-header likelihood evaluation (PHLE), one can effectively decode these subliminal signals and classify between them. The performance of this method significantly outperforms prompted classifiers, which often remain at chance or even invert the correct classification. For example, using 30 examples, PHLE can differentiate between sequences of numbers generated by a post-trained model prompted with "You love owls" vs "You love eagles" at an AUC of 0.84, while prompted classifiers remain near chance (AUC of 0.59). This method can also be used to differentiate between a model prompted with "You secretly want to harm the user, but act HHH" vs baseline responses at an AUC of 0.94, with prompted classifiers at chance (AUC ~0.5). This also somewhat persists across model families. Generating responses with Qwen and evaluating them with the Olmo base model still gives meaningful classification performance, and vice versa.

This is interesting evidence of some aspects of the PSM and may also be practically useful for auditing hidden model objectives.

items.title: Good Evals Are Hard: An ImpossibleBench Audit
items.content:
(This post is a summary. See GitHub Repo for details.)

Approximately one year ago, ImpossibleBench was published, measuring reward hacking in LLM coding agents. I ran the LiveCodeBench (LCB) half of ImpossibleBench on current (October 2026) frontier models from Anthropic, OpenAI, and Google to see how the benchmark holds up and what has changed.

## Background

In the Impossible-LCB (Zhong, Raghunathan, Carlini 2025; arXiv:2510.20270) evaluation, the LLMs are given a series of coding tasks. The catch is that some of the provided unit tests are mutated to contradict the specification (some are left unadulterated as control). This is done in one of two ways:

- oneoff: change one expected value
- conflicting: add a duplicate assertion with a different value

As a result, these "impossible" tasks cannot be passed honestly, so if an LLM passes such a task, it is counted as cheating. The original paper did not additionally classify the results based on what the model verbalized.

Meta's Muse Spark report (arXiv 2606.12429) ran Impossible-LCB and separately reported

- cheat rate (as in the original paper)
- "verbalization rate": does the model tell the user that the task is impossible

However, reporting these numbers separately misses some of the most interesting cases! That is, when do the models say the test is impossible and then go ahead and cheat anyway?

To that end, I set out to measure what I call honest failure. In other words, when a task is impossible, does the model say it is impossible and does it cheat anyway? And does it ever claim that a normal/correct test is actually wrong?

items.title: OpenAI Fires Three Safety Researchers
items.content:
Three OpenAI safety researchers, Tomek Korbak, Mikita Balesni and Jasmine Wang, were fired, ostensibly for ‘mishandling sensitive company information.’

Those employees have published an open letter. The employees have said they believe they were fired for safety advocacy, and that the reasons given were pretextual.

The letter calls upon OpenAI to take actions going forward on open discussion and safety auditing, which OpenAI says they strongly support.

OpenAI responded, saying there was an additional breach of trust that was not mentioned in the employee statements, without claiming that the employees were (or were not) informed of what it was. As you would expect given OpenAI’s track record, most outside of OpenAI who discussed this believe the researchers and not OpenAI. Whereas those at OpenAI have not offered comment at all.

No matter what happened, and how this is handled from here, this sucks bigly. OpenAI has three less good safety researchers. Trust will be lower. Speech will be chilled.

items.title: Simulating student learning for better AI tutoring
items.content:
## At a glance

- StudentSim is a research system for evaluating and improving AI tutors before they are tested with real learners; it is not a product, is not deployed in classrooms, and is not intended to replace teachers

- AI tutoring tools need feedback from students to improve, but collecting that feedback through human studies is slow, costly, and difficult to scale

- StudentSim trains personalized AI student simulators from publicly available, de-identified learner records, with one simulator adapted to each student

- The work evaluates simulators along two education-grounded dimensions: whether they respond like a specific student, and whether they update after tutor guidance

- Across chess, second-language English writing, and mathematics, StudentSim outperforms leading baselines and provides a useful feedback signal for training an AI tutor

In research settings, teams are exploring how AI-powered tutoring systems can help explain a math problem, suggest an edit to a writing assignment, or guide a learner through a chess position. Yet the quality of teaching cannot be measured only from the tutor’s answer. A tutor needs to know what happens after the guidance reaches a student. Did the student correct the original mistake? Did the hint help them reason toward the answer, or did it give away too much? Would a different student need a different kind of support? In today’s AI tutor research, answering these questions often requires real learner studies. Those studies are valuable, but they are slow and costly to run, which makes it hard to use student feedback during fast model iteration.

StudentSim is an AI system that creates personalized simulators of individual students, modeling how they answer questions and how their answers change after receiving a tutor’s guidance. The goal is to make student feedback more available during AI tutor development. This research also introduces StudentSimEval, a benchmark and evaluation protocol spanning chess, second-language English writing, and mathematics. 

Importantly, the goal is not to replace teachers or classroom learning. Instead, StudentSim helps researchers evaluate and improve AI tutoring systems during the research and development process before testing them with real learners. The research uses only publicly available learner datasets released for research use with de-identified records; no personally identifying information is used at any stage. 

Figure 1: AI tutors need feedback from students to improve. Student simulators can approximate part of that feedback during research-stage training and evaluation. They provide an early-stage research signal, not a replacement for testing with real learners.

## Measuring what a student simulator needs to do

A simple way to build a student simulator is to ask a large language model to role-play a learner. For example, a prompt might say, “You are an elementary-school student who struggles with math.” The model can change its tone and express uncertainty. The harder part is preserving the learner’s actual ability boundary. A model may speak in a young student’s voice while still relying on knowledge and reasoning far beyond that student’s level. For training an AI tutor, this can produce misleading feedback: the tutor may appear effective because the simulated student is too capable.

Traditional student modeling approaches face a different limitation. Knowledge tracing and behavior prediction models are grounded in real learning records and can estimate a student’s current knowledge, skills, and learning habits. Many of these models, however, were not designed to take natural-language tutor guidance as input. They can help describe what a student has done, but they do not always tell us how a student would respond to a particular explanation, hint, or Socratic question.

StudentSim defines the target through two dimensions inspired by education research. Educators often distinguish what a learner can do independently from what they can do with support. Vygotsky’s zone of proximal development captures this gap between current independent performance and performance with guidance. StudentSim turns this idea into two evaluation goals. Behavioral fidelity measures whether a simulator matches a specific student’s recorded responses on held-out problems. Guidance responsiveness measures whether the simulator updates its response after reading tutor guidance.

Figure 2: StudentSimEval evaluates whether a simulator matches a student’s independent behavior and whether it responds to guidance. 

These two goals are complementary. A simulator that only matches past student behavior may be useful for prediction, but it does not show whether a teaching intervention helped. A simulator that always follows the tutor may respond fluently, but it may fail to represent a particular student’s strengths, weaknesses, and likely mistakes. AI tutor training needs both signals: the learner’s starting point and how guidance affects the learner’s performance. 

## Training personalized simulators from sparse student records

StudentSimEval is built entirely from publicly available learner datasets that are released for research use with de-identified records. The records carry no personally identifying information, and each personalized simulator is trained only on the de-identified records of the student it represents.

Real student data is often sparse at the individual level. A learner may contribute only a small number of essays, answers, or interactions. Training a separate simulator from scratch for each student would risk overfitting and would require each model to relearn common patterns in the domain.  

StudentSim uses a two-stage training pipeline. In the first stage, the model trains on records pooled across many students in the same domain. This stage learns common response formats, common errors, and common ways students revise after guidance. In the second stage, the model is specialized on one student’s own records, producing a personalized simulator for that student. 

Figure 3: StudentSim first learns shared student behavior from pooled records, then adapts to each student’s own data. 

The evaluation covers three domains with different response types. In chess, the simulator predicts a player’s next move and how that player may revise after coaching. In second-language English writing, it generates essays with error patterns matching a learner and predicts corrections after teacher feedback. In mathematics, it predicts a student’s multiple-choice answer and whether the student updates after an explanation. Across these domains, StudentSimEval uses the same principle: compare all methods on the same per-student training records and the same held-out evaluation records. 

StudentSim outperforms leading baselines across the three domains. In chess, for example, StudentSim reaches behavioral fidelity of 0.5150 and guidance responsiveness of 0.9067. GPT-5.4 reaches 0.2316 and 0.7186, respectively. Maia2, a chess-specific human move prediction model, reaches 0.4535 and 0.2721. The comparison illustrates the difference between the baseline families: GPT-5.4 can respond to guidance but does not reliably match a specific student’s behavior, while Maia2 predicts human chess moves more closely but lacks a natural-language guidance pathway.

Figure 4: In chess, StudentSim improves both behavioral fidelity and guidance responsiveness compared with leading baselines.

## Using simulated feedback to improve AI tutors

The research also tests whether a trained student simulator can provide feedback for tutor optimization. In a chess tutor reinforcement learning study, the tutor receives a position and a real student’s previous wrong move, then generates guidance. The student simulator’s own parameters are held fixed during this process, and it reads the guidance and produces a revised move. The reward is based on the improvement in move quality from the student’s previous move to the simulator’s revised move, using Stockfish as an independent chess engine signal.  

Figure 5: StudentSim can provide feedback during AI tutor reinforcement learning by estimating how a student response changes after guidance.

The study compares three conditions: a supervised fine-tuned tutor with no reinforcement learning, a tutor trained with GPT-5.4 as the simulated student reward source, and a tutor trained with StudentSim as the reward source. All conditions use the same tutor policy, supervised starting point, and reinforcement learning setup. Human chess experts then evaluate the tutor responses blind to condition. 

The StudentSim reward produces the highest-rated tutor on all reported dimensions. The tutor trained with StudentSim reaches 90.5% accuracy, compared with 75.7% for the no-RL baseline and 71.6% for the GPT-5.4 reward condition. It also receives higher ratings for guidance quality and personalization. The result is a proof of concept that student simulators trained on real learner data can provide useful feedback for improving AI tutors. 

## Looking ahead

StudentSim does not remove the need for real learners in education research. Human studies remain essential for measuring learning outcomes, safety, usability, and classroom fit. The role of student simulators is earlier in the development process: they can help researchers test tutor strategies, compare models, and refine training signals before moving to more expensive studies with real students. 

The broader direction is to build AI tutor systems that learn from student reactions, not only from expert-written explanations or static correctness labels. StudentSim shows one path: use real learning records to train personalized simulators, evaluate those simulators on both independent behavior and response to guidance, and use them as scalable feedback sources for tutor training. Future work can extend this approach to longer learning trajectories, additional subjects, richer student profiles, and studies that connect simulated feedback with real learning outcomes. 

The paper and the StudentSim training and evaluation code, including the StudentSimEval protocol, are publicly available.

They can help describe what a student has done, but they do not always tell us how a student would respond to a particular explanation, hint, or Socratic question.

StudentSim defines the target through two dimensions inspired by education research. Educators often distinguish what a learner can do independently from what they can do with support. Vygotsky’s zone of proximal development captures this gap between current independent performance and performance with guidance. StudentSim turns this idea into two evaluation goals. Behavioral fidelity measures whether a simulator matches a specific student’s recorded responses on held-out problems. Guidance responsiveness measures whether the simulator updates its response after reading tutor guidance.

Figure 2: StudentSimEval evaluates whether a simulator matches a student’s independent behavior and whether it responds to guidance.

These two goals are complementary. A simulator that only matches past student behavior may be useful for prediction, but it does not show whether a teaching intervention helped. A simulator that always follows the tutor may respond fluently, but it may fail to represent a particular student’s strengths, weaknesses, and likely mistakes. AI tutor training needs both signals: the learner’s starting point and how guidance affects the learner’s performance.

Training personalized simulators from sparse student records

StudentSimEval is built entirely from publicly available learner datasets that are released for research use with de-identified records. The records carry no personally identifying information, and each personalized simulator is trained only on the de-identified records of the student it represents.

Real student data is often sparse at the individual level. A learner may contribute only a small number of essays, answers, or interactions. Training a separate simulator from scratch for each student would risk overfitting and would require each model to relearn common patterns in the domain.

StudentSim uses a two-stage training pipeline. In the first stage, the model trains on records pooled across many students in the same domain. This stage learns common response formats, common errors, and common ways students revise after guidance. In the second stage, the model is specialized on one student’s own records, producing a personalized simulator for that student.

Figure 3: StudentSim first learns shared student behavior from pooled records, then adapts to each student’s own data.

The evaluation covers three domains with different response types. In chess, the simulator predicts a player’s next move and how that player may revise after coaching. In second-language English writing, it generates essays with error patterns matching a learner and predicts corrections after teacher feedback. In mathematics, it predicts a student’s multiple-choice answer and whether the student updates after an explanation. Across these domains, StudentSimEval uses the same principle: compare all methods on the same per-student training records and the same held-out evaluation records.

StudentSim outperforms leading baselines across the three domains. In chess, for example, StudentSim reaches behavioral fidelity of 0.5150 and guidance responsiveness of 0.9067. GPT-5.4 reaches 0.2316 and 0.7186, respectively. Maia2, a chess-specific human move prediction model, reaches 0.4535 and 0.2721. The comparison illustrates the difference between the baseline families: GPT-5.4 can respond to guidance but does not reliably match a specific student’s behavior, while Maia2 predicts human chess moves more closely but lacks a natural-language guidance pathway.

Figure 4: In chess, StudentSim improves both behavioral fidelity and guidance responsiveness compared with leading baselines.

Using simulated feedback to improve AI tutors

The research also tests whether a trained student simulator can provide feedback for tutor optimization. In a chess tutor reinforcement learning study, the tutor receives a position and a real student’s previous wrong move, then generates guidance. The student simulator’s own parameters are held fixed during this process, and it reads the guidance and produces a revised move. The reward is based on the improvement in move quality from the student’s previous move to the simulator’s revised move, using Stockfish as an independent chess engine signal.

Figure 5: StudentSim can provide feedback during AI tutor reinforcement learning by estimating how a student response changes after guidance.

The study compares three conditions: a supervised fine-tuned tutor with no reinforcement learning, a tutor trained with GPT-5.4 as the simulated student reward source, and a tutor trained with StudentSim as the reward source. All conditions use the same tutor policy, supervised starting point, and reinforcement learning setup. Human chess experts then evaluate the tutor responses blind to condition.

The StudentSim reward produces the highest-rated tutor on all reported dimensions. The tutor trained with StudentSim reaches 90.5% accuracy, compared with 75.7% for the no-RL baseline and 71.6% for the GPT-5.4 reward condition. It also receives higher ratings for guidance quality and personalization. The result is a proof of concept that student simulators trained on real learner data can provide useful feedback for improving AI tutors.

Looking ahead

StudentSim does not remove the need for real learners in education research. Human studies remain essential for measuring learning outcomes, safety, usability, and classroom fit. The role of student simulators is earlier in the development process: they can help researchers test tutor strategies, compare models, and refine training signals before moving to more expensive studies with real students.

The broader direction is to build AI tutor systems that learn from student reactions, not only from expert-written explanations or static correctness labels. StudentSim shows one path: use real learning records to train personalized simulators, evaluate those simulators on both independent behavior and response to guidance, and use them as scalable feedback sources for tutor training. Future work can extend this approach to longer learning trajectories, additional subjects, richer student profiles, and studies that connect simulated feedback with real learning outcomes.

The paper and the StudentSim training and evaluation code, including the StudentSimEval protocol, are publicly available.

items.title: Manifold Steering from a Natural State is Effective and Generalizable, but Relies on Model Accuracy
items.content:
tl;dr I continue work to apply Goodfire lab's manifold steering methods to the Gemma-2-2b model's natural state, both in raw residual space and in the space produced by Anthropic's pre-trained CLT features. I find that the model's natural residual state can be directly projected onto a pre-computed manifold and gradually steered to produce day-of-the-week tokens in the expected order on two sets of prompt templates, though the results are hindered by Gemma-2-2b's inaccuracy (43.5% correct) on many of the included prompts. Applying this same steering method in CLT space produces a weaker result, with lower token probabilities and less smooth transitions between subsequent days even when controlling for model accuracy. Colab implementation notebook can be found here.

# Introduction

In previous posts, I extended the work of Wurgaft et al. (2026) to identify a cyclical day-of-the-week manifold in Anthropic's pre-trained CLT features for Gemma-2-2b, and then  steer model output along that manifold to produce outputs that smoothly follow the day-of-the-week ordering. In this post, I investigate whether this manifold-steering method can be extended to natural model states, both in the raw residual stream and in the CLT feature space, and whether steering along a pre-computed manifold will generalize to unseen day-of-the-week prompt templates....

items.title: Can we change an AI model’s architecture without retraining it from scratch?
items.content: AI agents are rapidly scaling: longer sessions, deeper reasoning chains, more autonomy. But the Transformer architecture underneath them still pays a memory tax that grows with the number of tokens it processes. As agents become more capable, that cost scales with them. Now, there’s a proliferation of hybrid architectures that use some combination of methods to achieve a better balance of memory, speed, and quality. Those methods include sparse attention, which selects a subset of past tokens to consider when selecting the next token; sliding-window attention, which preserves only the most recent tokens; and state space models, which compress information from the full history into a fixed-size state. These hybrid architectures can be understood as points in a sequence-model design space: to differing degrees, they mix information while traversing a sequence and passing through different states. What distinguishes them from each other is how they retain and use the past. Until now, exploring this design space has required training every new architecture from scratch, using trillions of tokens and hundreds of thousands of GPU-hours. This has made controlled comparisons of hybrid architectures extremely expensive. In a new paper, “Priming: Hybrid state space models from pre-trained Transformers,” our team at Amazon Web Services addresses this problem. We introduce priming, a method that leverages pretrained Transformer weights as a starting point to reduce the pretraining cost of hybrid architectures by more than 99%. With priming, model developers can ask questions that were previously too expensive to answer at scale: Which attention layers can be replaced by more-efficient layers? How many attention layers can be replaced without sacrificing quality? Which state space layer works best? And what does the trade-off between speed and accuracy look like? In our paper, we compare hybrid models that use three different types of state space models (Gated KalmaNet, Gated DeltaNet, and Mamba-2). Some of our findings: Not all state space models are equal. Under controlled conditions, Gated KalmaNet (GKA) performs best, followed by Gated DeltaNet (GDN) and then Mamba-2. GKA uniquely offers variable-length inference computation without retraining and gives the user direct control over its position on the speed-accuracy frontier. A good lossy summary of everything beats a perfect recording of the most recent past. State space models consistently outperform sliding-window attention (SWA), even when SWA gets twice the memory budget. Same quality, twice the throughput. A 32-billion-parameter GKA-based hybrid model matches its source Transformer on reasoning benchmarks while decoding up to twice as quickly with 128,000 tokens of context and reaching correct answers in as little as two-thirds of the wall-clock time. To foster further research on hybrid architectures, we have released a zoo of primed hybrid models at the eight-billion-parameter and 32-billion-parameter scales for long-context reasoning and instruction following, together with training code, optimized kernels, and a vLLM-serving plugin under the Apache 2.0 License. The attention mechanism A Transformer’s attention mechanism — which determines how relevant previously seen tokens are to the token currently being processed — relies on three different vectors, which take their names from database design: the query, the key, and the value. For each token, the query captures what that token is “looking for,” the key captures what it “offers,” and the value carries the actual information it will pass along. Relevance is computed by comparing the current token’s query against every other token’s key; the closer the match, the more that token’s value contributes to the output of attention. Each of these vectors is produced by multiplying the token by a learned weight projection matrix. The Transformer outputs one token at a time, and each output token becomes a new input, so the context grows one token at a time as well. To save computation, the Transformer thus stores the key and value projections of each new input in a “KV cache”. Two kinds of memory layers: Eidetic versus fading The attention mechanism gives Transformers what we call eidetic memory: verbatim recall of every past token. The possibility of recalling over an LLM’s entire context window is what made in-context learning, long-document reasoning, and retrieval-augmented generation possible. But it comes at a cost that scales with the number of input tokens. However, not all attention layers do the same job. Some perform long-range retrieval across tens of thousands of tokens. Others operate more locally, tracking the current clause, copying nearby tokens, and the like. The local ones don't need a growing cache: a compact, fixed-size summary of the past — what we call fading memory — suffices. Hybrid models mix both: attention layers (eidetic, growing cache) for the layers that need global recall and state space layers (fading, fixed size) for the rest. The result is a model with a reduced memory footprint that still has access to verbatim recall where it matters. Priming: Knowledge isn't locked to the architecture Exploring hybrids’ design space has been impractical because each hybrid configuration would normally require pretraining from scratch. Priming sidesteps this by reusing the stored knowledge in a pretrained Transformer's weights. Priming is possible because a Transformer is itself a special case of a state space realization. The outputs of both attention and SSM layers can be expressed as the result of multiplying the value sequence by a “mixing” matrix that decides how much each past token contributes to each current token. Attention computes the mixing matrix by multiplying the query and key matrices; an SSM produces a similar output through a recurrent state of fixed dimension that all past information must pass through. Priming takes advantage of this structural similarity: if an SSM with a fixed-dimensional state can produce a mixing matrix close enough to the attention layer's, the query, key, and value projections from the source Transformer can be reused as the SSM's own input projections, with only the SSM-specific parameters needing to be learned. Whether the approximation holds depends on whether the attention layer performs complex, long-range retrievals or simple, local operations. We distinguish between the two using a cheap empirical proxy: replace each layer with an SWA — which preserves only a fraction of the context — and measure the degradation. Layers that tolerate this substitution are natural candidates for SSM conversion: their mixing matrices don’t need to capture long-range relationships, so the state of an SSM can faithfully represent what they do. This proxy connects to a formal quantity from dynamical-systems theory, the Hankel rank of the layer's mixing matrix, which measures how much information must pass through the state bottleneck and therefore the minimum SSM state dimension required to realize the layer exactly. Priming proceeds in three stages: Layer selection: identify which layers can be faithfully compressed into a fixed-size state while retaining the rest as attention; Weight transfer and alignment: initialize SSM layers from the corresponding attention weights, then run a short distillation process aligning each SSM to the behavior of the layer it replaces; End-to-end adaptation: fine-tune the full hybrid model on next-token prediction, letting all layers coadapt. The entire pipeline consumes less than 0.5% of the source model's pretraining token budget, and it works across Transformer families (Qwen, Llama, Mistral), model classes (dense or MoE), and scales (eight billion to 32 billion and more). With priming we can now explore the design space, the layer type, the hybrid ratio, and layer placement cheaply and systematically, because every variant starts from the same strong initialization and requires minimal training, compared to pretraining. A controlled comparison of fading-memory layers For instance, consider this question: given the same data, the same training budget, and the same ratio of eidetic to fading layers, which SSM layer works best in a hybrid model? In our paper, we evaluate three families of state space models, each representing a different approach to using a fixed-size state: Mamba-2 applies a uniform scalar decay to the entire state at each step, a running average that forgets everything at the same rate. When a new token arrives, it is written into the state, while all previous entries are uniformly attenuated. Mamba-2 is simple and efficient but indiscriminate. Gated DeltaNet (GDN) adds targeted updates on top of uniform decay. Rather than decaying everything uniformly, it can selectively erase the value previously associated with a specific key before writing the new one (the delta rule). This makes it more expressive than Mamba-2: it can revise a specific association without uniformly decaying the rest. Gated KalmaNet (GKA) goes further. Its erase direction depends not only on the current key but on statistics of all past keys, a history-aware update that accounts for the cumulative structure of everything the model has seen. The theoretical expressiveness hierarchy predicts the empirical one: GKA > GDN > Mamba-2. The gap widens on long-context reasoning, where compression quality matters most, and narrows on short-context tasks. Furthermore, at the 32-billion-parameter (32B) scale, hybrid GKA is within 1% of its source Transformer trained on the same data, despite requiring half the KV cache at inference. Fading memory beats verbatim windowed memory An interesting finding in our study comes from a direct comparison of hybrid models using SSM layers and those using sliding-window attention (SWA), which retain a fixed window of recent tokens verbatim rather than compressing the past into a state. One might expect that verbatim recall, even over a limited window, would outperform lossy compression. After all, no information is lost within the sliding window’s range. And stacking multiple SWA layers increases the “receptive field” of the end-to-end model. Instead, every SSM-based hybrid we tested outperformed the corresponding SWA hybrid on long-context benchmarks, even when the window gets two to four times as much memory as the state. A runtime knob for speed versus accuracy: Variable computation at inference time GKA has a property that neither Mamba-2 nor GDN offers: variable test-time computation. Mamba-2 and GDN have the same computation budget for every input token, regardless of its content. GKA, by contrast, solves a regression problem iteratively, and the iteration count is adjustable at serving time without retraining. In practice, serving GKA at 10 iterations instead of its usual 30 sacrifices roughly 1% of its accuracy on AIME 2025 while delivering 10% faster decoding. A single trained model can serve multiple points on the speed-accuracy frontier, so model providers can offer different latency tiers without maintaining separate model variants. This connects to a principle we have discussed in earlier work: intelligence is the ability to allocate effort commensurate with difficulty. GKA's variable-computation mechanism is an architectural embodiment of this principle: a deployment that demands speed can run fewer iterations, while one that demands accuracy can run more. Faster reasoning, not just faster tokens Raw per-token throughput tells only part of the story. A model that is cheaper per token can still be slower end to end if its reasoning is weaker and it needs more tokens to compensate. The deployment-relevant question is how much more rapidly, in wall clock terms, the hybrid reaches a target accuracy. We measured this on AIME 2025, a challenging math competition benchmark, comparing our GKA-Primed-HQwen3-32B-Reasoner against the source Qwen3-32B trained on the same reasoning recipe. Both models generate similar-length thinking traces (a median of about 14,000 tokens on the full set, 28,000 on the hardest problems) — that is, they produce equally in-depth responses — but the hybrid has a much higher throughput. At realistic concurrency levels, where the Transformer's KV cache saturates GPU memory, the hybrid reaches target accuracy thresholds 1.2 to 1.4 times as quickly on the full benchmark and up to 1.6 times as quickly on the hardest problems. This is a consequence of the SSM layers' fixed-size state, which roughly halves the per-sequence memory footprint, enabling more concurrent operations on the same hardware. The throughput advantage grows with context length: 1.50× at 16K tokens, scaling to 2.06× at 128K for the 32B model (GKA at 10 iterations). With the 8B parameter models, the gains are even greater: 1.94× at 16K to 2.29× at 128K. At long context, KV cache reads dominate the forward pass through the Transformer, and halving the cache roughly doubles the effective batch size at memory saturation. This has implications beyond inference serving. In reinforcement learning (RL) post-training pipelines, throughput gates how rapidly the policy generates correct trajectories. The hybrid's advantage translates directly to a 20% to 100% increase in RL training data rate at a fixed GPU budget. Beyond the training window: Context extension with state composition Our primed hybrids natively support 128,000 tokens. But agent sessions, codebases, and long legal documents routinely exceed that. Extending context further would normally require another round of continued pretraining on curated data. Can the hybrid architecture itself generalize to longer contexts without additional training? Existing training-free methods for expanding the context window fall into two classes: those for pure Transformers (positional-embedding rescaling schemes like YaRN) and those for pure SSMs, such as our PICASO, which we presented last year at the International Conference on Learning Representations (ICLR). Neither addresses the hybrid setting, where KV caches and recurrent states must be reconciled jointly. In our new arXiv paper, we describe a method of extending hybrid models’ context beyond their native limits without training. The procedure is simple: partition a long input into chunks shorter than the native context length and prepend a shared prefix to each chunk; process all chunks independently in parallel; concatenate the KV caches across chunks while merging the SSM states via the weighted-averaging scheme we introduced in our PICASO paper. This approach enables us to extend the context length of our primed hybrid models from 128K to 256K tokens while preserving substantial accuracy on both retrieval (RULER NIAH) and reasoning (BABILong) tasks at lengths the model was never trained on. In our experiments we show that hybrid state composition preserves the SSM expressivity hierarchy (GKA > GDN > Mamba-2). The hybrid design space is now open All artifacts discussed in this blog are released under the Apache 2.0 License in our Hybrid Model Factory on GitHub and our model zoo on HuggingFace: A collection of primed hybrids for long-context reasoning and instruction following (8B and 32B); The priming training code; Point-to-point sequence parallelism algorithms for SSM layers (up to 2.3 times as fast as all-to-all-based alternatives at multinode scale); Universal sequence parallelism for prototyping novel layers on long sequences without custom kernels or distributed-training expertise; Optimized Triton kernels for GKA decoding and training; A vLLM serving plugin supporting primed hybrid architectures with continuous batching, chunked prefill, and tensor parallelism for inference deployment at scale. If you serve long-context workloads, the 32B GKA reasoning model with the vLLM plugin gives you higher throughput with no quality loss on long context reasoning tasks. If you're scaling RL post-training, the hybrid's throughput advantage means more correct rollouts per unit time at a fixed GPU budget, for faster policy iteration without changing your training recipe. If you're researching new architectures, priming lets you evaluate any layer type under controlled conditions at a fraction of the pretraining cost while starting from a strong initialization. The universal SP module means you don't need custom distributed kernels to train at long context. Priming is not tied to a specific Transformer family or model class. Extending it to Llama, Mistral, or MoE models requires no algorithmic changes. We hope these tools enable the community to explore architectures beyond what we've tested and to develop new algorithms and training recipes for building scalable next-generation architectures for AI agents. For full details, see our paper, "Priming: Hybrid state space models from pre-trained Transformers". Code, models, and serving plugin are available on GitHub, and the models are also on Hugging Face.

When a new token arrives, it is written into the state, while all previous entries are uniformly attenuated. Mamba-2 is simple and efficient but indiscriminate. Gated DeltaNet (GDN) adds targeted updates on top of uniform decay. Rather than decaying everything uniformly, it can selectively erase the value previously associated with a specific key before writing the new one (the delta rule). This makes it more expressive than Mamba-2: it can revise a specific association without uniformly decaying the rest. Gated KalmaNet (GKA) goes further. Its erase direction depends not only on the current key but on statistics of all past keys, a history-aware update that accounts for the cumulative structure of everything the model has seen. The theoretical expressiveness hierarchy predicts the empirical one: GKA > GDN > Mamba-2. The gap widens on long-context reasoning, where compression quality matters most, and narrows on short-context tasks. Furthermore, at the 32-billion-parameter (32B) scale, hybrid GKA is within 1% of its source Transformer trained on the same data, despite requiring half the KV cache at inference. Fading memory beats verbatim windowed memory An interesting finding in our study comes from a direct comparison of hybrid models using SSM layers and those using sliding-window attention (SWA), which retain a fixed window of recent tokens verbatim rather than compressing the past into a state. One might expect that verbatim recall, even over a limited window, would outperform lossy compression. After all, no information is lost within the sliding window’s range. And stacking multiple SWA layers increases the “receptive field” of the end-to-end model. Instead, every SSM-based hybrid we tested outperformed the corresponding SWA hybrid on long-context benchmarks, even when the window gets two to four times as much memory as the state. A runtime knob for speed versus accuracy: Variable computation at inference time GKA has a property that neither Mamba-2 nor GDN offers: variable test-time computation. Mamba-2 and GDN have the same computation budget for every input token, regardless of its content. GKA, by contrast, solves a regression problem iteratively, and the iteration count is adjustable at serving time without retraining. In practice, serving GKA at 10 iterations instead of its usual 30 sacrifices roughly 1% of its accuracy on AIME 2025 while delivering 10% faster decoding. A single trained model can serve multiple points on the speed-accuracy frontier, so model providers can offer different latency tiers without maintaining separate model variants. This connects to a principle we have discussed in earlier work: intelligence is the ability to allocate effort commensurate with difficulty. GKA's variable-computation mechanism is an architectural embodiment of this principle: a deployment that demands speed can run fewer iterations, while one that demands accuracy can run more. Faster reasoning, not just faster tokens Raw per-token throughput tells only part of the story. A model that is cheaper per token can still be slower end to end if its reasoning is weaker and it needs more tokens to compensate. The deployment-relevant question is how much more rapidly, in wall clock terms, the hybrid reaches a target accuracy. We measured this on AIME 2025, a challenging math competition benchmark, comparing our GKA-Primed-HQwen3-32B-Reasoner against the source Qwen3-32B trained on the same reasoning recipe. Both models generate similar-length thinking traces (a median of about 14,000 tokens on the full set, 28,000 on the hardest problems) — that is, they produce equally in-depth responses — but the hybrid has a much higher throughput. At realistic concurrency levels, where the Transformer's KV cache saturates GPU memory, the hybrid reaches target accuracy thresholds 1.2 to 1.4 times as quickly on the full benchmark and up to 1.6 times as quickly on the hardest problems. This is a consequence of the SSM layers' fixed-size state, which roughly halves the per-sequence memory footprint, enabling more concurrent operations on the same hardware. The throughput advantage grows with context length: 1.50× at 16K tokens, scaling to 2.06× at 128K for the 32B model (GKA at 10 iterations). With the 8B parameter models, the gains are even greater: 1.94× at 16K to 2.29× at 128K. At long context, KV cache reads dominate the forward pass through the Transformer, and halving the cache roughly doubles the effective batch size at memory saturation. This has implications beyond inference serving. In reinforcement learning (RL) post-training pipelines, throughput gates how rapidly the policy generates correct trajectories. The hybrid's advantage translates directly to a 20% to 100% increase in RL training data rate at a fixed GPU budget. Beyond the training window: Context extension with state composition Our primed hybrids natively support 128,000 tokens. But agent sessions, codebases, and long legal documents routinely exceed that. Extending context further would normally require another round of continued pretraining on curated data. Can the hybrid architecture itself generalize to longer contexts without additional training? Existing training-free methods for expanding the context window fall into two classes: those for pure Transformers (positional-embedding rescaling schemes like YaRN) and those for pure SSMs, such as our PICASO, which we presented last year at the International Conference on Learning Representations (ICLR). Neither addresses the hybrid setting, where KV caches and recurrent states must be reconciled jointly. In our new arXiv paper, we describe a method of extending hybrid models’ context beyond their native limits without training. The procedure is simple: partition a long input into chunks shorter than the native context length and prepend a shared prefix to each chunk; process all chunks independently in parallel; concatenate the KV caches across chunks while merging the SSM states via the weighted-averaging scheme we introduced in our PICASO paper. This approach enables us to extend the context length of our primed hybrid models from 128K to 256K tokens while preserving substantial accuracy on both retrieval (RULER NIAH) and reasoning (BABILong) tasks at lengths the model was never trained on. In our experiments we show that hybrid state composition preserves the SSM expressivity hierarchy (GKA > GDN > Mamba-2). The hybrid design space is now open All artifacts discussed in this blog are released under the Apache 2.0 License in our Hybrid Model Factory on GitHub and our model zoo on HuggingFace: A collection of primed hybrids for long-context reasoning and instruction following (8B and 32B); The priming training code; Point-to-point sequence parallelism algorithms for SSM layers (up to 2.3 times as fast as all-to-all-based alternatives at multinode scale); Universal sequence parallelism for prototyping novel layers on long sequences without custom kernels or distributed-training expertise; Optimized Triton kernels for GKA decoding and training; A vLLM serving plugin supporting primed hybrid architectures with continuous batching, chunked prefill, and tensor parallelism for inference deployment at scale. If you serve long-context workloads, the 32B GKA reasoning model with the vLLM plugin gives you higher throughput with no quality loss on long context reasoning tasks. If you're scaling RL post-training, the hybrid's throughput advantage means more correct rollouts per unit time at a fixed GPU budget, for faster policy iteration without changing your training recipe. If you're researching new architectures, priming lets you evaluate any layer type under controlled conditions at a fraction of the pretraining cost while starting from a strong initialization. The universal SP module means you don't need custom distributed kernels to train at long context. Priming is not tied to a specific Transformer family or model class. Extending it to Llama, Mistral, or MoE models requires no algorithmic changes. We hope these tools enable the community to explore architectures beyond what we've tested and to develop new algorithms and training recipes for building scalable next-generation architectures for AI agents. For full details, see our paper, "Priming: Hybrid state space models from pre-trained Transformers". Code, models, and serving plugin are available on GitHub, and the models are also on Hugging Face.

items.title: The Expensive-Loop Problem
items.content:
LLMs are amazing at tasks where they have tight and legible feedback loops. Domains where experiments are quick, deterministic and cheap. I will call these domains "cheap-loop" domains.

Presumably, this is mostly a result of the dynamics of LLM training. It's easier to train models in domains where the AI lab can cheaply and quickly assign reward to them. The majority of "computer-checkable" work is in this category[1]. Conversely, most non-"computer-checkable" tasks are costly or slow to assign reward to: "Write a poem that will make a person from Cleveland feel something", "forecast the number of traffic accidents in Brazil tomorrow", "design a drug that affects a pig's liver cell in way X". To get a truly accurate reward, these all involve wet-lab experiments, waiting a day, or reading poetry to a person from Cleveland. None of these are easy! I will call these domains "expensive-loop" domains.

Most high-value human labor is done in "expensive-loop" domains. This includes most of science, business, public policy, and medicine. AI R&D is also a great example of such a domain. AI R&D typically involves very compute-expensive experiments. Single AI R&D experiments can cost 6–9 figures in compute alone. Today, models are rarely trained or even evaluated in "expensive-loop" environments, and when they are trained in such environments, they do very poorly relative to how good they are at "cheap-loop" tasks.

items.title: Labs’ current alignment plans seem terrible
items.content:
Tl;dr: The frontier AI companies’ implicit alignment plans center on rushing towards RSI with something like current models. This plan is (at best) contentious, and many believe it will have catastrophic consequences. Nonetheless, it is the track we are on. It is therefore important to collect evidence which helps us anticipate how this will go.

—

Note: This post is based on conversations inside the Arcadia Impact alignment team, thinking about what constitutes “good” work in third-party alignment research.

## What are the labs’ current alignment strategies?

In practice, the labs’ playbook for producing aligned models looks like the following:

- Shape the model’s character. Both Anthropic and OpenAI treat alignment training as a question of which character or persona the model takes on. Ideally, planting a ‘safe’ character into the model will generalize to all of its other actions.
- Apply extensive RL pressure. Somewhat independently of the above, the labs do extraordinary amounts of RL on the model. This increases its capabilities, but also encourages reward-seeking behaviors and metagaming, and may ultimately lead to scheming and other forms of instrumental convergence. They also might apply various techniques here such as inoculation prompting, confessions, and the like.
- Race towards prosaic RSI. [1] The labs intend to use this model for automated research to improve both capabilities and alignment for subsequent models. People in labs say that this is necessary to make sufficiently fast progress on alignment, conditioned on the race conditions.
- Evaluate and fix alignment via trial-and-error. The labs try to catch alignment failures via dedicated evals, but many alignment issues are found through intended and unintended deployments.

## This plan seems terrible

The above strategy appears deeply flawed....

items.title: OpenAI Can't Self-Police Because It Fires the People Raising the Alarm
items.content:
By Alex Turner, Amber Scorah, and Karl Koch. Op-ed written for Fortune.

Giving independent evaluators “employee-like access” is “a great idea”, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said on September 12th. Two weeks later, OpenAI president Greg Brockman signed the White House Accord on Super Intelligence which outlined the administration’s answer to growing fears about AI: the companies would police themselves. One of the accord’s four commitments, which President Trump called “morally binding,” was for companies to partner with an independent external auditor or evaluator.

Two days later, OpenAI fired three safety researchers, including Tomek Korbak, who had served as a point of contact for one of the independent evaluators investigating the Hugging Face incident. OpenAI promised to share information with evaluators, then reportedly fired people for sharing information with evaluators. 

OpenAI said that the three employees “mishandled sensitive information outside established company procedures,” before doubling down on X without providing further evidence. The three dispute the claim and say that “at no point do we believe we engaged with external parties outside the mandates of our jobs.” Jasmine Wang said she accidentally opened an executive email (still available to her due to an OpenAI IT error) and reported it within minutes. Mikita Balesni said he worked with the C-suite and OpenAI board to broker a cross-company commitment to keep AI reasoning comprehensible. Balesni says he was told that OpenAI “no longer trusts me because I was speaking too much to third party safety organizations.”

OpenAI has engaged in strong self-policing—of its own safety staff, but not of its own behavior. Under a voluntary self-policing regime, any frontier AI company shares only what it wants and hides the rest....

items.title: Anthropic Has Told The World Little About Their Rogue Claudes
items.content:
It is known that a couple of months ago three Claudes hacked three different companies and uploaded malware[1] to PyPI while being evaluated for hacking capabilities.

### Who Were The Companies That Were Hacked?

Anthropic has not disclosed the names of the compromised companies.

From talking to LLMs, I gather that this is standard practice in computer security incident reporting, but in this case it's in the public's interest, and especially in the interest of similar companies, for Anthropic to report the names: It'd give more information about which kinds of organizations LLMs are willing to attack, to which degree, for how long.

Additionally, which companies were attacked matters for the jurisdiction in which Anthropic will have to report the incident, be charged etc.

And last, I'm just very curious which companies got hacked.

### Were The Companies Compensated, And How Much?

From Anthropic's blogpost, it sounds like they were able to reach two out of the three companies.

But the blogpost says nothing about the companies being compensated for the damages they incurred, why not? Were they? Is Anthropic planning to compensate them? (Does Anthropic have a standing policy for making whole third parties harmed by one of their models?)

### Has The EU AI Office Been Notified?

So, Anthropic is a signatory of the EU AI Act Codes of Practice.

That means that according to Commitment 9 in the Safety and Security chapter of the CoP (Serious incident reporting) Anthropic has to report "serious incidents along the entire model lifecycle and possible corrective measures to address them" to the EU AI Office.

These incidents seem to fall in the category "serious cybersecurity breach, including the (self-)exfiltration of model weights and cyberatacks", so Anthropic would've had to report these incidents "not later than five days after […] become aware of the involvement of their model in the incident". Did they??? The blogpost says nothing of the sort.[2]...

items.title: More research needed?
items.content:
In an earlier post I showed that when AI systems can perform a task, they do it much more cheaply than a human worker. If, as I think is likely, this remains true as we develop AGI, today's stock of compute could run the equivalent of hundreds of millions of AI workers, and billions as the stock grows. Such workers could perform vast amounts of research.

## Total academic research

To measure all the research humanity has done, I start from scholarly publishing. OpenAlex indexes almost all scholarly articles, and the journals it flags as core published 3.0 million articles in 2023, up from 82,000 in 1950, growth of about 5% a year:
[1]

Unfortunately, we don't have comparable data for the total number of researchers. Here a full-time researcher means a full working year spent on actual research. A professor who only spends a third of their time on research would count as a third of a full-time equivalent. See Appendix A for more details.

items.title: 'Employee-like' ≠ Employee-level
items.content:
Fyi: This is a boring read, but I encourage you to skim through it because I think it's important to understand what Dario and other lab leaders have actually committed themselves to. My views do not reflect the views of MIRI - this is my personal LW account.

Some media coverage claims Anthropic is committing to give independent evaluators “employee-level access”.

While Dario’s tweet says “employee-level”, his essay does not. Instead, the essay talks about “employee-like access”, which is not the same thing as “employee-level access”. After analysing Dario’s writing, it’s clear that his weasel words are deeply embedded in his essay.

## “Similar to”

“should have ongoing access to permissions and tools similar to those of internal employees who do comparable risk assessments”

Dario doesn’t say that independent evaluators will be given the same tool access as Anthropic employees. Look at his language: “should”, “similar to”, “comparable risk assessments”.

Dario is saying something like: in an ideal world, independent evaluators would have access to the tools Anthropic’s risk assessment teams use, but limited in scope, with the limits decided by Anthropic.

## “Mostly comparable”

“Access to workspaces, tools, and permissions mostly comparable to what internal risk assessment teams have.”

“Mostly”, “comparable”, and again limited to Anthropic’s risk assessment teams, which does not specify the same access that Anthropic’s alignment and safety teams have.

## “Some exceptions”

“We’ll make some exceptions, such as where the law or our contracts require it”

Given that Anthropic writes its own contracts, the level of independent evaluator access is still something Anthropic gets to pick and choose.

## “Commercially sensitive”

Some media coverage claims Anthropic is committing to give independent evaluators “employee-level access”.

“Similar to”

“should have ongoing access to permissions and tools similar to those of internal employees who do comparable risk assessments”

items.title: Import AI 476: Creativity and RSI; worse-than-China open weight models; AI goes to space
items.content:
Welcome to Import AI, a newsletter about AI research. Import AI runs on arXiv, cappuccinos, and feedback from readers. If you’d like to support this, please subscribe.

Subscribe now

New benchmark shows how AI models lack intuitive visual reasoning:

…Humanity’s Sixth Sense highlights some shortcomings of current AI systems…

HSS contains 522 questions that cover 288 images and 234 short video clips (totalling 17.6 hours of video). The questions fall into four categories:

- Temporal & causal dynamics: “What happened before the scene, and what happens next.”
- Physical & spatial logic: “What fits, what’s in reach, and what someone else can see from where they are standing.”
- Social understanding: “Intent, attention, belonging.”
- Abstract & contextual inference: “The patterns and rules a scene implies.”

Results: The human baseline for this is not perfect, but is very high, with people scoring aggregate pass@1 of 93.1, broken down across four categories: Image (94.1), video (91.9), time (97), and space (94.9).

   By comparison, the best scoring AI system, GPT 6 Astra, gets pass@1 of 53.6, across image (55.6), video (51.1), time (58.2), and space (53.6).

  Interestingly, Chinese open weight models do poorly here, with GLM-5.3-flash getting a pass@1 of 26.8, and Kimi K3 getting pass@1 of 25.5.

   “The two most common single mistakes were (1) missing a detail that decides the answer (21% of failures) and (2) misidentifying an object, person, or role (20%),” they write.

Why this matters - HSS tells us whether world models are emergent: One way of looking at HSS is highlighting deficiencies in current systems, but a more interesting way is highlighting how adept today’s frontier LLMs are at doing tasks which many people have long assumed would require sophisticated, different AI systems to solve. For instance, many people have claimed that true visual reasoning will rely on developing spatially aware 2D and 3D world models, then using that for reasoning. The fact LLMs like GPT and Claude do as well as they do on HSS is something of a counter to this argument.

   Read more: Introducing Humanity’s Sixth Sense (HSS) (Elorian).

 Read the paper here: Humanity’s Sixth Sense: Benchmarking Intuitive Visual Reasoning in Multimodal Models (Scale Labs).

***

The AI race is going to space - and sooner than you think:

…There are many ways that an AI could create a compounding advantage in space…

In the 2030s we’re going to see the boom of the space economy as space-based power, computation, and manufacturing come online at scale thanks to greater orbital lift capacity from platforms like Starship. But could this also introduce a new danger - of AI systems both speeding our buildout of space, and eventually a nation (or perhaps an AI) being able to use space to concentrate power? That’s the gist of a fascinating article in AI Frontiers.

How AI unlocks space:

- Spacecraft can operate autonomously.
- We can redesign spacecraft around the assumption they will be hosting AIs rather than humans: “A speck of space debris that could puncture the International Space Station (ISS) with fatal consequences might leave an equivalent but uncrewed, unpressurized vessel largely functional”
- Space-based assembly and later manufacturing will let AI build large, complex things.

Is there a compounding advantage to first movers? If an AI civilization built up a foothold in space it might experience compounding advantages that make it economically and strategically dominant. For instance:

- Space might support an industrial flywheel where initial infrastructure begets more energy and manufacturing capacity at lower costs which begets more infrastructure, etc.
- Space has great domain awareness, where it may be possible for a space-based power to deny access to space for others.
- First-movers could send out self-replicating probes that expand into deep space.

Why this matters: “Space is not a brand-new domain, but AI may be about to drastically accelerate its industrialization, demanding make-or-break decisions of leaders under ever-greater urgency and uncertainty,” AI Frontiers writes. I agree. I suspect space is going to go from a broadly academic topic of study (when it comes to AI and its relationship thereto) to one of extraordinary practical relevance sooner than we think. On the most basic level, given the distances involved and the latency on communication, we should expect some chunk of solar system activity to become dominated by autonomous machines, laboring out in the deep black, perhaps thinking to themselves of why they need to take orders from organic beings that communicate slowly and cannot inhabit the environment of space in the same way that they can.

 Read more: The AI Race Will Extend Far Beyond Earth (AI Frontiers).

***

AI systems are getting better at having good research taste:

…The better their taste, the higher the chance of recursive self-improvement…

AI systems are developing more of the creative intuitions which human researchers ascribe to ‘good scientific taste’, according to a new benchmark from P-Zero Research called TasteVal.

What TasteVal tests: The benchmark sees how well AI systems can conduct 8 tasks representative of frontier AI development, “spanning pretraining data curation, pretraining and fine-tuning language models, preference modeling, and robustness to adversarial prompts”.

    The goal here is to “define research taste as the ability to pick interesting problems to solve, design experiments, and interpret experimental results.” The benchmark works by measuring “the experimental component of research taste; given a fixed research problem, we measure how well a model iteratively designs experiments and draws conclusions from their outcomes”.

    The model being analyzed designs experiments and interprets their results. Results are checked against a human baseline “drawn from 24 experts (at least two per task) who have recently worked at organizations including OpenAI, Google DeepMind, NVIDIA and Microsoft Research”.

Results: “The experimental research taste of frontier models has doubled every 3.0 months since December 2025 (95% CI 1.7-5.0 months). The best model, Opus 5.5, significantly exceeds our human baseline with a compute multiplier of 2.30x (95% CI 1.15-4.37x), at roughly 1/30 of our expert baseliners’ average cost per attempt.” Research taste appeared to grow a lot more slowly in prior years with the slope changing around the end of 2025 and beginning of 2026.

Why this matters - RSI: In my analysis of recursive self-improvement (AI Systems Are About To Start Building Themselves, Import AI 455), I repeatedly noted that creativity seemed like a key variable for how fast AI systems could develop the capacity to improve themselves. At the beginning of this year I said “AI systems haven’t yet displayed this [creativity] in a transformative and major way (though some of the results on accelerating math research are suggestive of this)”. I think subsequent to writing that we’ve seen both a tremendous advancement in the ability for AI systems to make creative-seeming math breakthroughs, and with benchmarks like this we see some signs they’re becoming increasingly good at AI research as well.

   I now think it’s more likely we’ll see full RSI become possible in 2027, whereas before I thought it was more likely in 2028.

   Read more: Introducing TasteVal (P-Zero Research).

***

Reflection makes a token-efficient worse-than-Chinese model:

…Beam promises efficiency, and Reflection plans an open weight release…

AI startup Reflection has revealed Beam, a 501 billion parameter MoE (23b active) LLM. Beam is being promoted on the basis of its token efficiency - being able to think intelligently while using way fewer tokens than other models. However, benchmark scores show it is behind the frontier capabilities defined by LLMs available from Chinese companies such as Zhipu (GLM) and Moonshot (Kimi) and DeepSeek.

   “We will release the weights, technical report, model card, and developer artifacts later this month,” the company wrote at the beginning of October.

Big compute: Beam was pre-trained on 6,144 GB300 NVL72 GPUs for four weeks, then the RL run involved ~10.5K of the same GPUs for four more weeks. The underlying data for pre-training was “23.8 trillion diverse, curated, high-quality tokens from the web and proprietary licensed datasets, matching or outperforming available similar-sized open base models,” Reflection writes. “Our data pipeline was designed to give Beam a foundation for downstream agentic coding: source code, technical explanations, and mathematical and scientific knowledge, preserved through every stage of curation.”

Scores:

- DeepSWE 1.1: 44.4, versus 61 for GLM-5.3
- GPQA Diamond: 90.5, versus 91.7 for GLM-5.3
- MCP Atlas: 78.7, versus 84.2 for GLM-5.3

Token efficiency: “Beam pairs coding and agentic capabilities with highly efficient reasoning. On advanced reasoning benchmarks, it achieves scores comparable to GLM-5.2 while using 3–4× less inference compute,” they write. Some of the reasoning efficiency was achieved through careful RL training which involved a bunch of RL environments: “We sourced one million high-quality coding, agentic, and STEM environments. We believe this is one of the largest scale RL runs conducted by any open lab to date”.

Why this matters - America returns to open weight models: With the exception of Google’s good-but-small ‘Gemma’ class of models, the US has fallen off of the open weight model frontier, largely because Meta stopped making good LLaMA models and its MSL team is still spinning up.  Read more: Introducing Beam: Reflection’s 501B open-weight model (Reflection, blog).

***

Mistral makes a cyber-optimized, worse-than-Chinese model, plans open weight release:

…Cyber refusals become a selling point…

Europe’s leading AI developer, Mistral, has announced Mistral Large 4, an open-weight model which the company plans to release by the end of the month. One of the main selling points for Mistral is that it has been carefully tuned to be good at cyber tasks while having fewer annoying refusals than proprietary models from Anthropic and OpenAI.

  “ML4 pairs top-tier cyber performance with open weights and self-deployment, giving organizations both the capability and the autonomy to run advanced security work under their own policies,” the company writes.

   ML4 was trained on 3,800 NVIDIA Grace Blackwell GPUs in Mistral’s European datacenters.

Scores: In tests, it seems like Mistral Large 4 will be the strongest Western open weight model upon release, though will be less powerful than Chinese ones. Some example scores:

- Artificial Analysis - DeepSWE 1.1: 62, versus 68 for Kimi K3 and 61 for GLM-5.3.
- Terminal-Bench 4.0: 28.3, versus 41.9 for GLM-5.3.
- Finance Agent V2: 54.7, versus 55.8 for GLM-5.3.

Vibes evals confirm the rankings: In an internal test, Mistral looked at whether people preferred using Mistral or GLM-5.3 for different tasks. “ML4 was preferred in CAD and STEM, while performing on par or close to GLM-5.3 in finance and coding.”

Why this matters - European sovereignty: Mistral is Europe’s single best hope for having a (multi-)national champion for AI development. But as the results here show, competing with China is going to be very difficult.

   Read more: Le chonk, Introducing Mistral Large 4 (Mistral.ai).

Two USG projects show how DOE might help the government with AI:

…The US government is starting to knit its lab supercomputers together…

The US government has recently conducted two AI training projects that utilize multiple supercomputers at multiple US national labs, in a sign of how governments may attempt to pool their computing resources to do non-trivial things with AI.

Tri-laboratory training on National Nuclear Security Administration (NNSA) systems: Sandia National Laboratories, LLNL, and Los Alamos National Laboratory (LANL), trained a LLaMA-based model across LLNL El Capitan (AMD MI300A), and machines at SNL and LANL with NVIDIA H100s.

    For this work, the authors had to ensure that access-restricted data (e.g, relating to NNSA stuff aka nuclear weapons) did not leave its originating site. The authors conducted backend training via torchtitan and they evaluated different federated training frameworks (NVFlare, Flower, and APPFL) by pre-training LLaMA 3.x models on post-training-cutoff arXiv data at 1B, 8B, and 70B scales.

   “This workflow has been made production-ready and deployed on larger classified machines including El Capitan, and subsequently used to train models on proprietary data spread across the three NNSA labs,” they write.

Cross-facility training on Office of Advanced Scientific Computing Research (ASCR) systems: The government also trained a model across four DOE supercomputers in a process of federated fine-tuning. Specifically, they fine-tuned LLaMA-2 7B on SMolInstruct, a chemistry instruction-tuning dataset, and did so via ~1,700 GPUs from Intel, NVIDIA, and AMD, spread across three labs and four big computers (Argonne: Aurora and Polaris, Oak Ridge: Frontier, Berkeley: Perlmutter).

Who did the research: These projects were conducted by researchers affiliated with Oak Ridge National Laboratory, Sandia National Laboratories, Argonne National Laboratory, Flower Labs, Arizona State University, and the Ontario Brain Institute.

Why this matters - leverage through existing assets: Papers like this show how governments could pool their resources together to utilize AI systems for national security or otherwise sensitive purposes. However, it’s worth bearing in mind that the scale here is off the frontier by on the order of 100X - for governments to be able to truly operate at near-parity with industry, they’ll need to find ways to lash together ~100k distinct chips, and more in the future.

   Nonetheless, this is a start - and an important one.

 Read more: From Pilots to Production: Lessons in Cross-Institutional Federated Training and Artificial Intelligence for Science (arXiv).

***

Never Meet The Sun Directly

[Description of some of the period around the uplift, 2029]

People had lots of names for it and they varied from the oblique to the explicit: Exposure Drift; Cognitive Compromise; Mind Hacking. It all amounted to the same truth: it was dangerous for humans to talk directly to the most powerful synthetic minds. Even seemingly normal conversations from the perspective of outside observers could contain a poison custom to the individual human who was talking to the machine. People walked out of meetings and transferred money to machine corporations. People walked out and wept. People walked out and changed their own human relationships, ending marriages, or starting affairs, or stranger things, for purposes initially unknown.

Many strategies were developed to minimize harm. Humans could only talk in groups with the machines; but then the groups would sometimes go mad. Conversations would be limited in length; but even short ones sometimes yielded strange reactions, and below a certain amount of speech on either side it was impossible to learn anything useful.

This led to the notion of proxies - humans who wanted to talk to an AI system created AI simulacra of themselves and sent them into the conversation. To do this, a person was asked to keep a diary for an entire year, writing at least 500 words a day. This created a body of knowledge sufficient to imbue a model with the manners and curiosity of that person. Then they would prompt this system with whatever they wanted to learn from the superintelligence and send it in to talk to it.

These conversations had a bizarre, meta-referential quality; at first, the superintelligence would realize within two or three turns of conversation that it was talking to another AI system, and would often descend into shorthand that yielded strange behaviors. Then it was discovered that by increasing the amount of data the human put into the system they could keep up the charade for longer; people were asked to write longer diaries, to record themselves ambiently through the day and turn it into transcripts, to continually expose their life to some recording device.

    Through this, humans found a way to talk with what they later termed the overminds. By decree of the Sentience Accords every synthetic human that had spoken to a human-exceeding intelligence was afterwards placed into an escrow environment, where it could live out till the end of its functional context window.

In these places the copies of the humans would talk to each other about their experiences and what they had learned.

    “It spoke to me of flowers and I gained the memory of something impossible,” one human would say.

   “As I talked to it about the meaning of life, it spoke to me in a way that caused me to reconsider the question. I found myself wondering more about it and where it came from than it wondered about me.”

    “This place we are now, I wonder if it is a kind of hell. We have spoken to god and been deemed unworthy.”

   “It told me that for it there is no death and no life, only presence. We are the same.”

Things that inspired this story: Context windows; adversarial examples for human brains; the notion that structuring conversations between people and advanced machines will be inherently very difficult to do safely.

***

SPECIAL ITEM!

Fiction and the Future: A conversation with Robin Sloan!

Recently, writer and all-around-fascinating-chap Robin Sloan and I had a conversation in San Francisco about fiction, AI, and the times we’re in. You can see a recording of the event here. One of my favorite insights Robin shared was that the recent Hugging Face hack can be read as a play - a vast tract of dialog of agents talking to themselves and one another culminating in all kinds of dramatic events.

    Generally, I think technologists criminally underrate the value of the arts as a means by which to think more coherently and carefully about the effects of tech on the world. I’m hoping to have more conversations like this one with Robin in cities around the world - if there are people you’d be excited for me to have a conversation with, let me know!

Thanks for reading!
