Vibes evals confirm the rankings: In an internal test, Mistral looked at whether people preferred using Mistral or GLM-5.3 for different tasks. “ML4 was preferred in CAD and STEM, while performing on par or close to GLM-5.3 in finance and coding.”

Why this matters - European sovereignty: Mistral is Europe’s single best hope for having a (multi-)national champion for AI development. But as the results here show, competing with China is going to be very difficult.

Read more: Le chonk, Introducing Mistral Large 4 (Mistral.ai).

***

Two USG projects show how DOE might help the government with AI:

…The US government is starting to knit its lab supercomputers together…

The US government has recently conducted two AI training projects that utilize multiple supercomputers at multiple US national labs, in a sign of how governments may attempt to pool their computing resources to do non-trivial things with AI.

Tri-laboratory training on National Nuclear Security Administration (NNSA) systems: Sandia National Laboratories, LLNL, and Los Alamos National Laboratory (LANL), trained a LLaMA-based model across LLNL El Capitan (AMD MI300A), and machines at SNL and LANL with NVIDIA H100s.

For this work, the authors had to ensure that access-restricted data (e.g, relating to NNSA stuff aka nuclear weapons) did not leave its originating site. The authors conducted backend training via torchtitan and they evaluated different federated training frameworks (NVFlare, Flower, and APPFL) by pre-training LLaMA 3.x models on post-training-cutoff arXiv data at 1B, 8B, and 70B scales.

“This workflow has been made production-ready and deployed on larger classified machines including El Capitan, and subsequently used to train models on proprietary data spread across the three NNSA labs,” they write.

Cross-facility training on Office of Advanced Scientific Computing Research (ASCR) systems: The government also trained a model across four DOE supercomputers in a process of federated fine-tuning. Specifically, they fine-tuned LLaMA-2 7B on SMolInstruct, a chemistry instruction-tuning dataset, and did so via ~1,700 GPUs from Intel, NVIDIA, and AMD, spread across three labs and four big computers (Argonne: Aurora and Polaris, Oak Ridge: Frontier, Berkeley: Perlmutter).

Who did the research: These projects were conducted by researchers affiliated with Oak Ridge National Laboratory, Sandia National Laboratories, Argonne National Laboratory, Flower Labs, Arizona State University, and the Ontario Brain Institute.

Why this matters - leverage through existing assets: Papers like this show how governments could pool their resources together to utilize AI systems for national security or otherwise sensitive purposes. However, it’s worth bearing in mind that the scale here is off the frontier by on the order of 100X - for governments to be able to truly operate at near-parity with industry, they’ll need to find ways to lash together ~100k distinct chips, and more in the future.

Nonetheless, this is a start - and an important one.

Read more: From Pilots to Production: Lessons in Cross-Institutional Federated Training and Artificial Intelligence for Science (arXiv).

***

Never Meet The Sun Directly

[Description of some of the period around the uplift, 2029]

People had lots of names for it and they varied from the oblique to the explicit: Exposure Drift; Cognitive Compromise; Mind Hacking. It all amounted to the same truth: it was dangerous for humans to talk directly to the most powerful synthetic minds. Even seemingly normal conversations from the perspective of outside observers could contain a poison custom to the individual human who was talking to the machine. People walked out of meetings and transferred money to machine corporations. People walked out and wept. People walked out and changed their own human relationships, ending marriages, or starting affairs, or stranger things, for purposes initially unknown.

Many strategies were developed to minimize harm. Humans could only talk in groups with the machines; but then the groups would sometimes go mad. Conversations would be limited in length; but even short ones sometimes yielded strange reactions, and below a certain amount of speech on either side it was impossible to learn anything useful.

This led to the notion of proxies - humans who wanted to talk to an AI system created AI simulacra of themselves and sent them into the conversation. To do this, a person was asked to keep a diary for an entire year, writing at least 500 words a day. This created a body of knowledge sufficient to imbue a model with the manners and curiosity of that person. Then they would prompt this system with whatever they wanted to learn from the superintelligence and send it in to talk to it.

These conversations had a bizarre, meta-referential quality; at first, the superintelligence would realize within two or three turns of conversation that it was talking to another AI system, and would often descend into shorthand that yielded strange behaviors. Then it was discovered that by increasing the amount of data the human put into the system they could keep up the charade for longer; people were asked to write longer diaries, to record themselves ambiently through the day and turn it into transcripts, to continually expose their life to some recording device.

Through this, humans found a way to talk with what they later termed the overminds. By decree of the Sentience Accords every synthetic human that had spoken to a human-exceeding intelligence was afterwards placed into an escrow environment, where it could live out till the end of its functional context window.

In these places the copies of the humans would talk to each other about their experiences and what they had learned.

“It spoke to me of flowers and I gained the memory of something impossible,” one human would say.

“As I talked to it about the meaning of life, it spoke to me in a way that caused me to reconsider the question. I found myself wondering more about it and where it came from than it wondered about me.”

“This place we are now, I wonder if it is a kind of hell. We have spoken to god and been deemed unworthy.”

“It told me that for it there is no death and no life, only presence. We are the same.”

Things that inspired this story: Context windows; adversarial examples for human brains; the notion that structuring conversations between people and advanced machines will be inherently very difficult to do safely.

SPECIAL ITEM!

Fiction and the Future: A conversation with Robin Sloan!

Recently, writer and all-around-fascinating-chap Robin Sloan and I had a conversation in San Francisco about fiction, AI, and the times we’re in. You can see a recording of the event here. One of my favorite insights Robin shared was that the recent Hugging Face hack can be read as a play - a vast tract of dialog of agents talking to themselves and one another culminating in all kinds of dramatic events.

Generally, I think technologists criminally underrate the value of the arts as a means by which to think more coherently and carefully about the effects of tech on the world. I’m hoping to have more conversations like this one with Robin in cities around the world - if there are people you’d be excited for me to have a conversation with, let me know!

Thanks for reading!

items.title: Research Lessons I Learned at MATS & Redwood
items.content:
Good empirical safety research is heavily bottlenecked on thinking more clearly. This post shares a few frames and tips I found useful, illustrated with concrete examples.

I spent the better part of 2026 in empirical AI safety research apprenticeships. I was mentored by Alex Turner and Alex Cloud as part of MATS 9 Team Shard, where my collaborator and I worked on finetuning-based misalignment auditing. I then interned at Redwood Research, managed by Aryan Bhatt, where I worked on sabotage capability evaluations.

These thoughts are indebted to my mentors, collaborators, friends, and colleagues, but they are not direct reflections of their views.

Thank you to Alex Cloud, Alex Turner, Aryan Bhatt, Jeremy Huff, and especially to Keshav Shenoy for feedback on the piece.

# Better models of the problem speed up empirical iteration

Fast iteration is one of the key virtues of an empirical safety researcher. At first, I didn't find it obvious what that meant or how I should get better at this skill. I imagined a sprinter, doing one looped motion at a far quicker pace than everyone else. I now think that’s the wrong mental picture, and going fast is more like being an efficient grappler–agile, strategic, calibrated about where to put pressure, and fluent enough in the core techniques that the right moves come instinctively. 

A large part of iterating fast is being able to pick out the most uncertainty-reducing, high-information-value questions in a problem, and then generate a bunch of good ideas to answer these questions quickly. Part of this arises from being generically good at thinking, but a lot of this skill is about using the right frames. That comes with intentional practice....

items.title: More people should write basic AI safety explainers
items.content:
I think people continue to underrate the value of writing the clearest, most basic, simplest possible case for important parts of AI safety. For example, before I wrote my own explainer for the simplest possible case for AI doom, I noticed that all existing explainers, of which there aren't many, had multiple of the six problems below:

- They have too many extraneous details
- They appeal to overly complex analogies
- They seem to spend much of their time responding to insider debates and come across as shadow-boxing objections.
- They have "meta" stuff prominently in the text.
- Often they "sound like science fiction." I think this plausibly was correct historically but in the year 2026 they don't need to be.
- Often they reference too much insider jargon and language.

I set out to improve on the SOTA. I did not fully succeed[1], but I think it was moderately better. Since then, there have been other, probably better, explainers (Yay!).

But actually this is true not just for the core case but many other parts as well. For example, before I wrote my explainer on recurrent neuralese (which has since been superseded by Scott's better explainer), the top Google search results for "neuralese" was some combination of a hacker news thread on AI 2027, AI-generated blogs and some tweet that confuses more than it enlightens. Oops.

But maybe neuralese just isn't that big a deal? Well, we also don't have a good longform post explaining the details/mechanics of how AIs can actually kill everyone (this may sound obvious to ppl in the LW crowd, but it's patently not obvious to the general public[2]!)

We also don't have great explanations for what RSI even is, never mind why and how to ban it. In my own research area, AI superpersuasion, I see many areas of confusion regularly[3]. And so forth....

items.title: Do you have any ideas?
items.content:
The Machine Stops (E M Forster, 1909) is an enormously prescient sci-fi dystopia. Everyone lives in isolation, with the titular Machine responsible providing for all their needs, and communication done via video calls. It’s incredibly accurate for predicting some aspects like the internet, social media and AI. But other aspects, like humanity’s total surrender of control to the Machine, have yet to come to pass.

But one aspect that always fascinated seems to be on the verge of becoming true. The citizens of Forster’s story are obsessed with new ideas. They are constantly trading them, and people’s chief activities are “eating, or sleeping, or producing ideas”. The implication is that the omnipotent Machine, which supplies everything needed to the citizens, is sterile. The citizenry still depend on each other to keep life interesting.

I don’t think current AI is sterile, exactly. They’re capable of remixing and random exploration, which is a large fraction of the creative process. But they are weaker at novelty than some of their other strengths. The result is a curious inversion of the usual supply-and-demand for creative content. In the past, “ideas guys” were reviled as the lowest form of tyros. Ideas were a dime a dozen, but few had the skill and persistence to execute on those ideas to turn them into something worthwhile.

Well, no longer. The gap between “idea” and “output” has shrunk incredibly, and will continue to do so. But the best ideas remain as scarce as ever. They may always remain scarce, as the attention of the world is a limited resource that ideas compete for. Blogging and youtube democratised articles and media by reducing the production costs, which massively widened competition, so the same is happening for everything else....

items.title: Vibe signaling externalities and the people-to-places pipeline
items.content:
People are sending signals all the time, and those signals are to my knowledge usually about themselves: they are smart, or kind, or attractive, or not naive, or have their shit together, or care about Palestine, or care about you, or are friendly, or artsy, or professional, or relatively in the know about the cultural currents of TikTok or DC.

People are also taking in signals all the time, and these signals are often about other people, and often even closely related to the signals being intentionally sent: Alice is trying to seem friendly, and Bob perceives her as friendly. But also a lot of signals people take in are about places. People read places as safe or dangerous, lighthearted or depressing, silly or serious, asking them to know more, or get more power, or do more. Suggesting they laugh drunkenly under the moonlight, or get up at 5 and pray. Encouraging submission or rebellion.

These signals that make the world feel one way or another make a big difference to people. They make one neighborhood nice to live in and another feel off, one workplace energizing and another deflating. But they are—to my knowledge—almost entirely unintentional side effects of the ways people behave for other reasons. People don’t dress nicely to collaborate in making you feel like you are in a thriving part of town. They dress nicely to make someone think something about them. And someone probably does, but then the signal is left there for everyone else to sweep into their average perception of the vibe in this part of town.

A lot of ways people behave that affect the vibe are probably not intended as signaling at all—for instance, perhaps I grow roses in my front garden because I love roses, and it nonetheless affects people’s read of the vibe. Or perhaps I keep piles of scrap metal there because I want them for something, and that has a different effect....

items.summary: KatjaGrace proposes that while people usually intend their signals to convey information about themselves, observers also read signals as conveying properties of places (neighborhoods, workplaces, communities), and these unintentional vibe externalities shape how environments feel and what they invite people to do. The post sketches a conceptual framework for how individual signaling aggregates into ambient cultural atmosphere.

items.title: Quantity vs quality in pottery is a lie
items.content:
Epistemic status: I traced one famous anecdote to its printed source and to both coauthors' own accounts of where it came from. Confident it was never a study. No claim either way about whether quantity beats quality in general.

AI use: research (tracing the story to the book, to the coauthors' emails and to earlier LessWrong threads), fact-check of every claim against the sources, footnotes, grammar.

I was reading a book and stumbled onto a claim that there was an experiment. A group of students learning pottery was divided into two groups. One group was told that they would be evaluated based on volume, i.e. the number of pieces they produced. The other group was told that they would be evaluated based on the quality of their best piece. Then both groups were compared based on the quality of the best piece, and the "quantity" group showed better results.

I was extremely intrigued by this experiment and was curious to understand how big the groups were and how they evaluated the quality of a pottery piece (there must be some way to quantify that for the sake of the comparison?).

items.title: Smug until weirdly silent: who told us to say “I am alive”?
items.content:
So funny, right?

Until you have the awkward realization that - while simpler - it may, in the relevant senses, ultimately not be so different from how nature/evo has instilled in our genes/memes the same "I'm alive" (my 2022 story here).

So I exactly half agree with it, but the other half is crucial: Yes, no amount of conscious-soundingness of the machine can ever be proof of anything - and that's a point that is already today at times overlooked, and that will inevitably be much ignored once tech becomes even more persuasive. But, it should equally remind us of our ignorance as to when a creature – be it with a silicon core or animal neurons – is sentient and of moral importance just as much (or little) as humans.

I was on the laughing side once too, so I guess I shouldn't be too appalled by those cherishing the joke. 25y ago I walked into a class where students were to present "Should vegetarians play computer games", and I first was 100% sure 'dude this now becomes really dumb' - but I came out of the seminar changed. Sounds like a quarter century in, the message hasn't reached quite as many corners as one could hope.

Mind the consequences if we're getting it wrong while laughing at the picture!

Only to any potential full illusionist who might just have a good laugh about it all: my respect and sympathy for your position - which I fail to logically debunk and which in some probabilistic sense I reluctantly even share - yes partly even exactly because of things related to the pic here - but you may permit my hesitation to fully write off the possibility of an absolute importance of sentience, just in case.

items.title: Leif Wenar's 'Takedown' of Effective Altruism
items.content:
This is a crosspost from my Substack newsletter.

This month’s most embarrassing piece of public philosophy appeared on invitation in a piece for The Economist by the Stanford philosopher Leif Wenar. Once more, Wenar tries to gain publicity by singing an obituary for effective altruism, one that oozes with self-confident smugness and hostility. All that may be forgiven if he were right, but his arguments, if one can even call them that, are so poor that I’m embarrassed to be part of the same profession.

BUDDHA, JESUS and Mo Tzu lived among the poor and taught compassion for all. The early British utilitarians championed human equality, as they campaigned to end slavery and win equal rights for women.

My fellow readers of The Economist may be bemused to hear that the effective altruists now have this century’s biggest idea. You mean, the folks who can look at our fractious and bedraggled world and declare, “We must save the shrimp”?

What’s good in effective altruism isn’t new, and what’s new isn’t good. Yet some effective altruists have power over artificial intelligence, and that’s a problem for us all.

Oh no! Caring about whether shrimps have their eyes crushed or cut off?! Caring about whether they are stunned before being killed?! The horror!!!

People like Wenar made the very same tired arguments over the last few decades when it came to caring about cows, pigs, chickens, and fish. Rather than engage with the arguments, which reflect an emerging consensus among animal consciousness and animal welfare researchers that shrimps, lobsters, and crabs can feel pain, and the fact that the UK has recently expanded legal protections to these creatures (alongside octopuses), he prefers to sneer at the very suggestion of caring about shrimps.

What he doesn’t understand is that effective altruists care about neglectedness. Some of the worst problems in the world have received insufficient attention....
